_meta.description: Every NCERT concept × every sphere = a concrete bridge analogy. Parth selects the best bridge for each child based on sphere_affinity and provisional_telos.
_meta.structure: concept_id → sphere → { hook, example, best_for_telos[], puzzle_id? }

astronomy_cosmology.hook: Earth travels 2πr in one orbit. If you know Earth is 150 million km from the Sun, how far does it travel in a year?
astronomy_cosmology.example: Orbital circumference = 2π × orbital radius. Pi appears in every circular orbit in the universe.

arts_interdisciplinary.hook: The nautilus shell spirals outward by a fixed ratio at every turn. A circle cut into that spiral traces pi.
arts_interdisciplinary.example: Harmonic series on a guitar string: the frequencies are multiples that circle back — pi hides in the Fourier transform of any musical tone.

cricket.hook: Roll a cricket ball forward one full rotation along a ruler. Measure how far it travelled. Divide by the ball's diameter.
cricket.example: Every circular object contains pi in the relationship between its size and the distance it covers in one rotation.

philosophy_logic.hook: 4 × (1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + 1/9 - ...) = π. Why does an endless sum of odd-number fractions give you the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter?
philosophy_logic.example: The Leibniz formula connects the discrete (integers) to the continuous (circles). What does that mean about the nature of mathematics?

mathematics.hook: Draw a circle. Measure its diameter with a ruler. Now roll a coin of that diameter around the circle's edge. Count how many times it rotates.
mathematics.example: The answer is always π — regardless of the circle's size. This scale-invariance is the deep fact.

music.hook: A whole note gets 4 beats. A half note gets 2. A quarter note gets 1. An eighth note gets half a beat. Why are musical notes called fractions?
music.example: Time signatures in music are fractions: 3/4 time means 3 quarter-notes per bar. Reading music IS reading fractions.

cooking.hook: A recipe calls for 3/4 cup of flour. You want to make half the recipe. How much flour do you need?
cooking.example: Every kitchen calculation involving recipes uses fractions: doubling, halving, converting cups to tablespoons.

astronomy_cosmology.hook: Jupiter takes 12 Earth years to orbit the Sun. Saturn takes 29.5 years. What fraction of a Saturn year is a Jupiter year?
astronomy_cosmology.example: Orbital period ratios are fractions. Ancient astronomers discovered planetary ratios before they had decimal notation.

eastern_wisdom.hook: Aryabhata calculated the length of a year as 365 days, 6 hours, 12 minutes, 30 seconds. How would you write that as a fraction of a day?
eastern_wisdom.example: Ancient Indian astronomers worked in fractions of a day and a year centuries before the decimal system spread globally.

astronomy_cosmology.hook: The Moon falls toward Earth every second — but it also moves sideways fast enough that it keeps missing. What keeps it in orbit?
astronomy_cosmology.example: Orbital motion is free-fall with enough sideways velocity to keep curving around the planet. The same force that drops an apple keeps the Moon circling.

cricket.hook: A cricket ball thrown horizontally and one dropped straight down from the same height — which hits the ground first?
cricket.example: Both hit at the same time. Horizontal motion and vertical fall are independent. This is why parabolic flight paths work.

philosophy_logic.hook: Newton said gravity acts at a distance — instantly, across empty space. Leibniz asked: how? Through what? This debate was never resolved in Newton's lifetime.
philosophy_logic.example: Action at a distance was philosophically disturbing — it implied something could affect something else without touching it. Einstein later replaced it with curved spacetime.

chemistry.hook: A plant weighs 1 gram when it sprouts. After six months it weighs 1 kilogram. Where did the extra 999 grams come from? Not the soil — the air.
chemistry.example: Plants build their bodies from CO₂ — a gas. The carbon in every leaf, every wooden plank, every fruit came from the atmosphere.

eastern_wisdom.hook: Ancient Indian texts describe how trees are alive — that they feel, breathe, and respond to the world. Modern science confirms: they process light into food. How?
eastern_wisdom.example: The Vrikshayurveda (ancient Indian tree science) described plant responses that modern plant physiology is still studying.

cooking.hook: Every vegetable you eat was once sunlight. The energy in your dal, your roti, your rice — all of it started as a photon hitting a leaf.
cooking.example: The caloric energy in food is captured solar energy, stored in chemical bonds. Digestion releases it back.

social_sciences.hook: When conditions change suddenly — a drought, a new predator, a disease — which individuals survive? Is it the strongest? The fastest? Or the best-fitted to the new conditions?
social_sciences.example: Natural selection works on variation. Without variation, there is nothing to select. The source of variation (mutation) is random — selection is not.

eastern_wisdom.hook: The Jain concept of anekantavada (many-sidedness of truth) says no single description of reality is complete. Evolutionary theory says no single trait is 'best' — it depends on the environment.
eastern_wisdom.example: Evolution is contextual fitness, not absolute improvement. An adaptation that helps in one environment can be lethal in another.

computer_science_ai.hook: Genetic algorithms in computers mimic evolution: start with random solutions, select the best, recombine and mutate them, repeat. The computer 'evolves' a solution it was never explicitly programmed for.
computer_science_ai.example: Evolution is an algorithm. It runs on populations, not individuals. The 'code' is DNA; the 'fitness function' is survival and reproduction.

eastern_wisdom.hook: Imagine a balance scale. An unknown weight on one side, known weights on the other. How do you find the unknown? You've just done algebra without numbers.
eastern_wisdom.example: Al-Khwarizmi described this in 830 CE — the balance-scale method for solving equations. The word 'algebra' comes from his title: al-jabr (restoration of balance).

astronomy_cosmology.hook: Astronomers calculate where a comet will be in 300 years. They have never seen it there. They use algebra — equations that model motion — to predict.
astronomy_cosmology.example: Prediction from equations is algebra's superpower. You can solve for the unknown (the comet's future position) from what you know (its current position and speed).

cricket.hook: A spinner bowls 100 deliveries in a Test match. 32 are dot balls, 40 are singles, 18 are boundaries, 10 are wickets. What is the probability of a wicket on the next ball?
cricket.example: Probability from frequency: if past data shows 10/100 = 10% wicket rate, we estimate the next ball has roughly 10% chance. But: past performance doesn't guarantee future outcomes.

biology_medicine.hook: A disease affects 1% of the population. A test for it is 99% accurate. You test positive. What is the probability you actually have the disease?
biology_medicine.example: Bayes' theorem: the answer is less than 50% — because false positives outnumber true positives when the disease is rare. This is why medical testing is statistical.

social_sciences.hook: If you flip a coin 10 times and get heads every time, what is the probability of heads on the 11th flip?
social_sciences.example: 50% — the coin has no memory. But humans feel it 'should' be tails. This error is the Gambler's Fallacy: confusing independent events with dependent ones.

cooking.hook: You burn 100g of wood. The ash weighs only 5g. Where did the other 95g go? And what about the energy that was released as heat?
cooking.example: Mass-energy conservation: the 95g became gas and heat. Neither disappeared — they changed form. The energy released equals the chemical energy stored in the bonds.

astronomy_cosmology.hook: A spacecraft launched toward Pluto has no engine after the initial burn. Yet it keeps travelling for 9 years. What keeps it moving?
astronomy_cosmology.example: Conservation of momentum: in a vacuum with no friction, an object in motion stays in motion. The energy put in at launch is still there — just as kinetic energy.

philosophy_logic.hook: Parmenides argued in 500 BCE: 'Nothing comes from nothing.' Lavoisier proved it with a scale 2300 years later. Was Parmenides doing physics or philosophy?
philosophy_logic.example: The conservation of mass is a philosophical principle before it is a physical law. The experiment confirms what pure reason had already suspected.

astronomy_cosmology.hook: Ancient astronomers modelled all planetary orbits as perfect circles — and were very nearly right. Earth's orbit is 98% circular. How close to a circle is a circle?
astronomy_cosmology.example: Eccentricity: a measure of how far an ellipse deviates from a circle. Earth's eccentricity is 0.017 — nearly perfect circle. Pluto's is 0.248.

arts_interdisciplinary.hook: Every circular arch in Mughal architecture had to be constructed without modern tools. How did the builders ensure the curve was mathematically perfect?
arts_interdisciplinary.example: Practical geometry: a circle is defined by a fixed center and constant radius. Any point on the circle is exactly that distance from the center. Builders used ropes.

cooking.hook: An electric cooker has a 2000W element. If you run it for 30 minutes, how much does it cost? What is 'watt' actually measuring?
cooking.example: Power = energy per second. A watt is one joule per second. Your electricity bill charges for joules (kilowatt-hours). Cooking is energy accounting.

biology_medicine.hook: Your heart generates enough electrical signal to be detected from your wrist. Neurons fire at up to 100 electrical pulses per second. Your body runs on electricity.
biology_medicine.example: Bioelectricity: the same principles (voltage, current, resistance) that govern circuits govern nerve impulses. The Nernst equation governs both.

computer_science_ai.hook: A cell has a membrane that controls what enters and exits, a nucleus that stores instructions, ribosomes that manufacture proteins from those instructions. Sound familiar?
computer_science_ai.example: The cell is a biological computer: membrane = firewall, DNA = program code, ribosomes = CPU executing code, mitochondria = power supply.

philosophy_logic.hook: Is a single cell alive? Is a virus alive? What is the minimum definition of life — and who decides?
philosophy_logic.example: Defining life is a philosophical problem disguised as a biological one. Every proposed definition (reproduction, metabolism, response to environment) has edge cases.

philosophy_logic.hook: Gandhi's satyagraha was a philosophical argument made without words: civil disobedience as a claim that unjust laws have no moral authority. Was it a political strategy or a philosophical proof?
philosophy_logic.example: Civil disobedience is a logical structure: if a law is unjust, obeying it validates injustice. Non-violent resistance exposes the contradiction in the oppressor's position.

social_sciences.hook: In 1900, Britain controlled 23% of Earth's land surface with 0.1% of its population. How is that possible? What makes empire economically sustainable — until it isn't?
social_sciences.example: Political economy of colonialism: extraction, asymmetric trade, currency control. The same mechanisms that made empire profitable made it politically unstable.
